coverage: overnight since the evening brief (~19:40 → 08:20 CEST)
headline: OpenAI dumps 722 AI-made math papers on GitHub; Russia pounds Kyiv on Putin’s birthday; Merz and Macron eye a deal to loosen the 2035 combustion ban.

stories.title: OpenAI dumps 722 math manuscripts from an unreleased model on GitHub — and mathematicians want receipts
facts: New public repo openai/math: 722 manuscripts in 372 result families, from an internal frontier model OpenAI hasn’t released (Apache-2.0). Released ~00:00 CEST.
OpenAI says the model was posed ~4,000 problems; the average accepted result used about three hours of ChatGPT Pro-equivalent thinking. Many, not all, proofs are formalised in Lean.

Claimed results include the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, a Riemann zeta zero-free region (Re(s) > 11/12) and the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties; 10 families come with abridged reasoning summaries.

Same model as last month’s Navier–Stokes blow-up proof. OpenAI told Scientific American almost every result came from a single prompt to a single agent, and that its own mathematicians don’t yet understand many of them.
The IAS advisory group (AGMAI) asked labs to stop testing open problems on proprietary models and to disclose model, prompts and compute per result; OpenAI gives averages and says it isn’t bound.
Reactions split: MIT’s Andrew Sutherland says treat single-agent claims as unverified — “We should ask for receipts”; Toronto’s Daniel Litt calls the release “a good thing for mathematics”.
stories.whyItMatters: Hundreds of machine-made results at once, from a model nobody outside can run, push the question of who checks and gets credit for AI mathematics from theory to practice.

stories.title: Russia hits Kyiv with missiles and drones on Putin’s 74th birthday, a night after Ukraine’s ~700-drone raid on Moscow
facts: Explosions in Kyiv from ~02:15 CEST with a second missile wave two hours later; two people were found dead after a fire at a garage cooperative in Darnytskyi district.
Hits in Obolon (non-residential site) and Podil (warehouses); a residential building was damaged in Kremenchuk and transport infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia.
The strike came hours after Zelensky said intelligence showed Russia preparing a massive attack.

The night before, Moscow’s mayor Sobyanin counted 650+ drones heading for the Moscow region plus 68 more downed en route; Russian authorities reported two dead — one of the largest raids on the capital of the war.
stories.whyItMatters: Both sides are now trading capital-scale strikes; expect more pressure on European air-defence deliveries.

stories.title: FAZ: Merz and Macron are lining up a swap — Paris drops its veto on softening the 2035 combustion phase-out, Berlin bends on “Made in EU”
facts: A joint Franco-German position paper is being drafted in the Chancellery and Élysée, to be presented before the EU summit at the end of next week.
Macron would stop blocking looser CO₂ fleet limits for cars; Merz would drop resistance to strict “Made in EU” rules in the Industrial Accelerator Act.
France leads a seven-country blocking minority (incl. Spain, Netherlands) on the car rules; the EP transport committee vote set for Monday was postponed.
Goal is to end the combustion ban by early 2027. China, meanwhile, attacked the Merz–Macron letter calling for new EU anti-coercion tools: “Protectionism cannot increase competitiveness.”
stories.whyItMatters: If it holds, the de facto end of the 2035 ban moves from a German wish to a Council majority within weeks.

stories.title: Coalition committee meets today for the first time in three months; Spiegel poll: two in three Germans call Merz’s chancellorship a failure
facts: Union and SPD leaders meet Wednesday on the reform course; no decisions on disputed items expected, possibly a timetable. SPD wants changes after the September state-election losses.
Flashpoints: Klingbeil’s planned sugar, tobacco and plastic taxes, a 2027 budget that may slip past year-end, pensions after 45 contribution years, and care-insurance finances.
Spiegel/Ipsos: 48% fully and 19% partly agree Merz’s chancellorship has failed (80% in the east); 58% back his resignation as chancellor and party leader.
stories.whyItMatters: Today shows whether the coalition resets after the AfD’s state-level gains or keeps drifting into open conflict.

stories.title: Hijacked .gh, .sl and .as registries let attackers mint real TLS certificates for Google and other big brands
facts: Google: attackers compromised the three country-code TLD registries, rewrote authoritative DNS for selected domains and passed CA domain-validation checks.
Unauthorised certs covered “several Google domains” plus, per Certificate Transparency logs, “several leading global brands and widely used online services” (unnamed).
Chrome blocked them via CRLSets and the CAs revoked Google’s; Google says the CAs did nothing wrong and Chrome users need not act.
Advice to domain owners: watch CT logs and publish restrictive CAA records — browser blocks don’t protect non-Chrome users, and Google can’t guarantee it found every domain.
stories.whyItMatters: Domain validation is only as strong as the registry above you — a reminder that CAA and CT monitoring aren’t optional.

stories.title: Anthropic opens Mythos-class cyber access to more defenders; Chrome 155’s patch list shows AI bug-hunting at scale
facts: Anthropic merged Project Glasswing and its Cyber Verification Program into three tiers — Defense, Red Team, Specialized — all with Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Mythos 5.1. Specialized is vetted with the US government.
Its numbers: Glasswing partners found ≥129,000 verified vulnerabilities Apr–Jul 2026 (>33,000 critical/high), plus 5,500 from Anthropic’s own open-source scanning.
Test: on CyScenarioBench every task was blocked without CVP; Red Team tier ran unblocked and solved 34 of 50.
Chrome 155 stable (6 Oct) carries four critical fixes; 12 of the critical/high bugs are credited to Anthropic’s Xinyang Ge “assisted by Claude”, two to OpenAI Codex Security.
stories.whyItMatters: Labs are now gating offensive capability by customer tier rather than refusing outright — and their models already show up all over browser patch notes.

stories.title: ZEIT: a hole in Sungrow’s inverter cloud put gigawatts of European solar one click from shutdown
facts: An ethical hacker got into user, management and admin accounts on the Chinese maker’s cloud platform in late August without a password and could have switched off plants or pushed malware Europe-wide.
At times about 18 GW was reachable via the platform; Germany alone has ~250,000 Sungrow systems with 7.8 GW peak output.
Experts warn a sudden loss of 3 GW can trigger blackouts. Sungrow closed the gap with a hotfix; authorities see a regulatory gap because such inverters barely count as critical infrastructure.
stories.whyItMatters: Distributed solar is now grid-scale, but its remote-control plane still sits in vendor clouds with consumer-grade security.

stories.title: FT: SpaceX wants to raise $40bn — mostly bonds — to buy Nvidia AI chips
facts: Per the FT’s sources: ~$10bn in bank loans and ~$30bn in bonds, led by Apollo, with Pimco in talks; closing expected in 2027.
Musk had already announced more Nvidia chips for xAI; companies didn’t comment and Pimco declined.
stories.whyItMatters: Debt-financed GPU buying on this scale is the kind of AI-capex leverage that bubble sceptics keep flagging.

facts.text: Kenya has its first Ebola case: a Kenyan who fell ill in DR Congo travelled to Nairobi via Kampala and died there on Monday (Bundibugyo strain, per WHO); 28 contacts are quarantined.

France’s school protests escalate: 250,000+ students, parents and teachers marched Tuesday amid tear gas and water cannon; unions joined, and 5,000+ people, many minors, have been detained in two weeks.
Hamburg–Hannover rail: the coalition agreed a Bundestag motion for a 109 km two-track new line (Vinnhorst–Meckelfeld) plus upgrades to the old route; committee today, plenum vote Thursday night.
Cabinet takes up Justice Minister Hubig’s digital-violence bill today: new offences for sexualised deepfakes and identity abuse, and wider protection against intimate images taken without consent.

Japan extradited a 28-year-old Russian alleged to be Qilin’s ransomware coder to Germany — rare, as Japan only has treaties with the US and South Korea. The case rests on a 2024 extortion of a German logistics firm.

Xbox lands GTA VI cloud-streaming rights at launch (not exclusive, and not to PCs, per Xbox strategy chief Matthew Ball); CEO Asha Sharma told staff the old Game Pass strategy sent Xbox into “freefall”.

OpenAI’s Decisions API is in public beta: POST /v1/decisions returns typed predicate/choice/score answers on text or images ~10× faster than Responses (gpt-6-luna only). Vercel AI Gateway adds confidence-based fallbacks.
Cursor Remote Control: follow and reply to agents running on your own computer from the Cursor iOS app; on by default except for Enterprise orgs, with a “keep this computer awake” option.
Claude for Google Workspace is in public beta for paid Claude users: a sidebar in Docs, Sheets and Slides with an “ask before edits” mode, plus connectors to edit Workspace files from Claude.
BSI now advises against Classic McEliece for new post-quantum projects after a paper cut a theoretical attack from well over 2^200 to ~2^114 operations; hybrid deployments aren’t practically at risk.
Wizards of the Coast’s D&D and Magic teams are joining the CWA union; their demand letter tells Hasbro to stop pushing generative AI and gives a 13 Oct deadline for voluntary recognition.

facts.text: Warriors beat a short-handed Lakers 124-98 in their preseason home opener at Chase Center; LA sat seven players including Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves. Rookie Yaxel Lendeborg stood out.
BVB keeper Gregor Kobel (contract to 2028) to Sport Bild: he can “very well imagine playing here for a long time” and a summer exit was “zero” topic; extension talks are expected soon.
